falas: Have you ever passed someone in need... and kept walking?
Not because you didn't care. Because you had so little yourself.
Sixteen centuries ago, at the gate of a frozen city, a young soldier had almost nothing left to give.
What he did with that almost-nothing... is still remembered, every eleventh of November.
His name was Martin. He was a soldier of Rome... young, and not yet baptized.
As a boy, he had asked to learn the faith. But the army claimed him first.
The winter of that year was cruel. The cold was taking lives.
Martin had already given away everything he owned... except his weapons, and his soldier's cloak.
One evening, he rode toward the gate of a city called Amiens.
At the gate sat a man with almost nothing on.
People walked past him. Some looked away.
Martin had no coin to give. So he drew his sword...
[pause] and cut his cloak in two.
He gave one half to the stranger... and wrapped himself in what was left.
Some who were watching laughed. A soldier in half a cloak looked foolish.
Others said nothing... and felt ashamed. They had done nothing at all.
That night, Martin dreamed.
He saw Christ, with a multitude of angels around Him...
and Christ was wearing the half of the cloak he had given away.
And Martin heard Him say: "Martin, who is still but a catechumen, clothed me with this robe."
[pause] A catechumen. Not yet baptized. Not yet a monk, not yet a bishop, not yet a saint.
Just a young man... who did not walk past.
Christ had said it Himself, long before:
"Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."
The Church counts this among the works of mercy: to clothe the naked.
Not a grand gesture. A cloak. Half a cloak.
[softly] Martin would later be baptized... become a monk... and a beloved bishop of Tours.
But the story people kept, for sixteen hundred years, is this one.
[pause] Let us pray.
Lord, open my eyes to the one at the gate.
When I have little, teach me to share it.
And when I am the one in the cold... clothe me with Your mercy. Amen.
